Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems

Leyang Shen Yaxin Gong Yang Zhang Chenxiao Fan Jiakai Wang Affiliation:  National University of Singapore Affiliation:  University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation:  Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba* Corresponding author Email: lshen@u.nus.edu    Dong Wang Yang Liu Fuli Feng Chun Kai Ling Tat-Seng Chua Affiliation:  National University of Singapore Affiliation:  University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation:  Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba* Corresponding author
Abstract

Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to intervene with a high-cost slow path. To unlock its steering intelligence, the ability to assess goal drift and generate effective interventions, we jointly train the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.

   

A Preprint

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM)-based agents (Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025) and multi-agent systems (MAS) (Wu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024) increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use (Schick et al., 2023) and inter-agent collaboration (Hong et al., 2024), spanning information seeking (Team et al., 2025), software engineering (OpenAI, 2025), and scientific discovery (Qu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). However, these systems are prone to goal drift, where agents deviate from the overall goal as execution unfolds (Arike et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2025; Laban et al., 2026). A single agent may persist along an unproductive chain of actions, while an agent in a MAS may prioritize its local objective over the collective goal. Goal drift can waste execution resources and lead to undesired outcomes, even when individual actions appear locally reasonable (Cemri et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a).

To keep agents on track and ensure goals are achieved during long-horizon execution, prevalent agent systems, such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025), employ planning and verification (Young, 2025; Anthropic, 2026b). As illustrated in Fig. 1, planning decomposes a goal into manageable subgoals (Wang et al., 2023), but execution may still deviate from the planned route. Verification checks whether the goal has been achieved before termination, but such post-hoc remediation can lead to irreversible consequences and costly retries. These limitations motivate a natural design of on-the-fly supervision, where an external agent monitors execution and steers the system back toward its goal when drift occurs, complementing planning and verification.

Such supervision is conceptually straightforward but challenging for the LLM backbone. It requires steering intelligence, the ability to assess execution against the overall goal, determine when intervention is needed, and generate actions that steer systems back on track. Such a capability is established in other goal-directed systems, such as direct supervision in organizations (Mintzberg, 1979), supervisory control of automated systems (Sheridan, 1992), and metacognitive monitoring and control in human cognition (Nelson & Narens, 1990). We bring this principle to LLM agent systems by building a steering agent and improving its steering intelligence through post-training.

Specifically, we define an observation space that exposes the task goal and execution context of the agent system to the steering agent. During execution, each observation update triggers a decision about whether and, if needed, how to intervene. These two demands motivate a natural design with fast and slow paths (Kahneman, 2011; Su et al., 2025; Lampson, 1983; Clark et al., 1989). The fast path estimates steering priority through a low-cost single-token prediction. A threshold on this priority controls activation of the slow path, which leverages more costly reasoning to generate steering actions. By separating fast judgment from deliberative generation, this design balances monitoring efficiency and steering effectiveness. We then improve the steering intelligence of the steering agent by jointly training the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective (Burges et al., 2005) for fast-path steering judgment with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) for slow-path action generation.

We evaluate our steering approach on information-seeking search tasks (Mialon et al., 2024; Ho et al., 2020) in both single-agent and multi-agent settings. Our single-agent experiments show that steering is challenging even for a capable LLM backbone, and that reinforcement learning substantially improves steering intelligence. Across seven question-answering benchmarks, zero-shot steering yields a performance gain of only 1.84 points, whereas the RL-optimized steering agent improves performance by 6.66 points with only 0.93 steering actions per task. Furthermore, the steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining, with steering at the highest frequency raising the gain to 17.11 points. In the multi-agent setting, we introduce the steering agent into a five-role multi-agent system (Xu et al., 2026). In this more challenging steering task, where zero-shot supervision degrades performance, the RL-trained steering agent achieves a gain of 5.34 points.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We characterize goal drift in single- and multi-agent systems, where local objectives can displace the overall task goal, and motivate on-the-fly supervision to keep execution on track.

  • •

    We develop a steering agent with fast intervention judgment and deliberative action generation, and improve its steering intelligence through reinforcement learning.

  • •

    We conduct experiments on both single- and multi-agent settings, where the steering agent demonstrates effective performance gains, strong generalizability, transferability, and controllability.

2 Related Work

2.1 LLM-based Agent Systems

LLM-based single- and multi-agent systems are increasingly applied to complex, long-horizon tasks, including information-seeking research (Manus, 2025; Team et al., 2025), software engineering (OpenAI, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and scientific discovery (Zhu et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026). However, as increasingly complex tasks require longer execution horizons, these systems may deviate from their original task objectives, a failure mode known as goal drift (Arike et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2025; Laban et al., 2026).

To better equip LLMs for long-horizon interaction and multi-agent collaboration, recent work has explored agentic post-training, particularly reinforcement learning (RL) (Chen et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2025). Long-horizon agentic RL optimizes LLMs end-to-end with tools on complex tasks requiring extended interaction (Gao et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026). Multi-agent RL jointly optimizes collaborating agents under shared task-level objectives, encouraging individual agents to contribute to overall task success (Liao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). However, long-horizon rollouts can make training computationally expensive (Gao et al., 2025), and RL fine-tuning can overfit to the training environment, affecting the generalization ability of the foundation model (Aissi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026b; Lv et al., 2026). In contrast, we keep the task-executing LLMs frozen and train an external agent to supervise execution and steer the system back toward its overall goal when drift occurs.

2.2 Goal Drift Mitigation

To mitigate goal drift during long-horizon execution, prevalent agent systems (DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Young, 2025; OpenAI, 2025) employ planning and verification to support reliable execution. Planning decomposes a goal into manageable subgoals that guide subsequent actions (Wang et al., 2023). Verification checks whether goals have been met before an agent declares completion, prompting further execution or revision when needed (Anthropic, 2026b; Lopopolo, 2026). However, a plan does not ensure reliable execution (Sinha et al., 2026), while verification may uncover deviations after substantial effort has already been spent.

These limitations motivate a natural on-the-fly supervision design, where an external supervisor monitors intermediate execution and intervenes when goal drift occurs. Recent work explores this idea with a primary focus on detection, identifying when and where an agent goes wrong (Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Baidya et al., 2026). SupervisorAgent (Lin et al., 2026) takes a step toward correction by prompting an external LLM, but it targets easily fixable issues such as errors and repetitive actions. Goal drift, however, is more challenging to detect and correct in real time, as it emerges gradually from locally plausible actions. In this paper, we address this challenge with a steering agent that jointly learns drift detection and correction through reinforcement learning.

3 Learning to Steer LLM-based Agent Systems

In this section, we begin by discussing goal drift that happens in both single-agent and multi-agent systems (Section 3.1). Then, we introduce our steering agent design (Section 3.2) and the reinforcement learning algorithm (Section 3.3).

3.1 Goal Drift in LLM-based Agent Systems

An LLM-based agent executes a task with an overall goal gg by interacting with an environment (Yao et al., 2023). At each step, the agent generates an action conditioned on gg and the interaction history, and receives environment feedback. A multi-agent system distributes this process across specialized agents, where each agent handles a temporary subgoal derived from gg, such as retrieving evidence or verifying an answer, and hands its output to subsequent agents. In both settings, execution unfolds as a sequence of temporary subgoals in service of the overall goal (March & Simon, 1958).

In LLM-based agent systems, goal drift appears when a temporary subgoal dominates the overall task goal (Arike et al., 2025), leading to unproductive actions that might be locally reasonable. Goal drift reduces execution efficiency by consuming resources on actions that contribute little to task completion. If the deviation remains uncorrected, the agent system may never finish the task or finish it with an undesired outcome.

For example, in multi-hop search tasks (Ho et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018), the agent needs to retrieve several distinct pieces of evidence and combine them to answer a question, which involves a sequence of temporary retrieval subgoals. A common failure mode is that the agent keeps searching over the same topic when key information has already been obtained. As shown in Fig. 2(a), the first search already identifies the actress required to answer the question. The agent spends three more searches on the same film instead of moving on to the next step, consistent with observed patterns of redundant and unproductive search (Liu et al., 2026a).

In a multi-agent system, where specialized agents collaborate on a complex task, goal drift arises similarly when an agent prioritizes its role objective over the overall task goal. A commonly observed failure mode is over-rejection, where a verifier falsely rejects results that already satisfy the task goal (Huang et al., 2024; Stechly et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). As shown in Fig. 2(b), the verifier repeatedly rejects the answers the searchers have delivered, leading execution to repeated revision rounds that can turn a successful execution into a failure. This reflects the verifier overweighting its own goal of admitting only answers beyond doubt.

3.2 The Steering Agent

To mitigate goal drift, we design a steering agent that supervises agent execution on the fly and steers it back on track before further effort is wasted, achieving efficient goal completion.

Steering Interface.

Consider an agent system executing a task with goal gg. We define an observation space 𝒪\mathcal{O} through a function OO that exposes the goal and available execution context, and an action space 𝒜steer={pass}∪𝒜int\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{steer}}=\{\mathrm{pass}\}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{int}}, where pass\mathrm{pass} lets execution continue and 𝒜int\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{int}} contains the interventions supported by the system. At steering decision tt, the steering agent reads the observation ot=O⁡(g,st)∈𝒪o_{t}=O(g,s_{t})\in\mathcal{O}, where sts_{t} is the underlying execution state that collects the goal and the interaction so far, and returns a steering action:

at∼πθ(⋅∣ot),a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid o_{t}\right), (1)

where the steering policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, realized by an LLM with parameters θ\theta, maps each observation to a distribution over 𝒜steer\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{steer}}. The system applies the sampled action ata_{t} before resuming execution. This steering interface can achieve different steering granularities depending on the observation and action spaces. For example, exposing every execution step of a single agent enables fine-grained supervision, while exposing only inter-agent handoffs enables coarse-grained supervision over a multi-agent system.

We formalize the steering process as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) (Sutton & Barto, 2018; Kaelbling et al., 1998), where the agent system being supervised acts as the environment. At decision step tt, the steering agent observes oto_{t} rather than the full execution state sts_{t}, takes the action ata_{t}, and the agent system transitions from sts_{t} to

st+1∼𝒯(⋅∣st,at),s_{t+1}\sim\mathcal{T}\!\left(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}\right), (2)

where the transition 𝒯\mathcal{T} is realized by the system resuming execution until the next observation update. The task reward RR is received when execution terminates and measures goal completion.

As shown in Figure 3(a), each observation update marks a state transition in observation space and triggers a steering decision. The steering agent then judges whether the current state needs intervention and generates the intervention when it does. These two demands split the agent into a fast path and a slow path (Kahneman, 2011; Su et al., 2025; Lampson, 1983; Clark et al., 1989). The fast path judges the need for intervention at low cost, and the slow path produces the reasoning and action for intervention. Both paths share the same LLM backbone parameterized by θ\theta.

Fast path.

To process each observation update at low cost, the fast path judges the need for intervention within a single LLM forward pass. It operates by estimating the steering priority of the current state, which measures how much a steering action at this state can change the final outcome. This allows the steering agent to achieve a larger impact with a fixed intervention budget. Specifically, the fast path measures steering priority vθ​(ot)v_{\theta}(o_{t}) by a yes/no judgment, which is calculated by reading the probabilities of the two tokens:

zθ​(ot)=log⁡pθ​(yes∣Pfast​(ot))−log⁡pθ​(no∣Pfast​(ot)),vθ​(ot)=σ⁡(zθ​(ot)),z_{\theta}(o_{t})=\log p_{\theta}(\texttt{yes}\mid P_{\mathrm{fast}}(o_{t}))-\log p_{\theta}(\texttt{no}\mid P_{\mathrm{fast}}(o_{t})),\qquad v_{\theta}(o_{t})=\sigma(z_{\theta}(o_{t})), (3)

where Pfast​(ot)P_{\mathrm{fast}}(o_{t}) denotes the fast-path LLM input built from oto_{t}, pθp_{\theta} is the token probability given by the shared LLM backbone, zθ​(ot)z_{\theta}(o_{t}) is the log-odds between the two tokens, and the logistic function σ\sigma normalizes it to steering priority vθ​(ot)∈(0,1)v_{\theta}(o_{t})\in(0,1).

We then follow Bengio et al. (2013) to trigger the slow path with a soft threshold on the priority:

It∼Bernoulli⁡(pt),pt=σ⁡(logit⁡(vθ​(ot))−logit⁡(τ)),I_{t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{t}),\qquad p_{t}=\sigma\!\left(\operatorname{logit}(v_{\theta}(o_{t}))-\operatorname{logit}(\tau)\right), (4)

where It∈{0,1}I_{t}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the slow path is triggered and τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1) is the trigger threshold. The function logit⁡(x)=log⁡x1−x\operatorname{logit}(x)=\log\frac{x}{1-x} is the inverse of the logistic function σ\sigma, mapping the priority and the threshold onto the log-odds scale. The soft threshold is a smoothed version of the hard rule 𝟏[vθ(ot)>τ]\mathbf{1}[v_{\theta}(o_{t})>\tau], whose trigger probability ptp_{t} exceeds one half once the priority exceeds τ\tau and approaches one as the gap grows. We write πθfast​(It∣ot)\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fast}}(I_{t}\mid o_{t}) for this trigger distribution, which represents the probability of entering the slow path given the observation oto_{t}.

Slow path.

Once triggered, the slow path conducts chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022) and generates a steering action. Let rtr_{t} denote the generated reasoning and at∈𝒜inta_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{int}} the resulting steering action, produced as one output sequence yt=(rt,at)y_{t}=(r_{t},a_{t}). The slow path can then be represented by an LLM auto-regressive generation process:

πθslow​(rt,at∣ot)\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{slow}}(r_{t},a_{t}\mid o_{t}) =pθ​(rt∣Pslow​(ot))​pθ​(at∣Pslow​(ot),rt)\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid P_{\mathrm{slow}}(o_{t}))\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid P_{\mathrm{slow}}(o_{t}),r_{t}) (5)
=∏ℓ=1|yt|pθ​(yt,ℓ∣Pslow​(ot),yt,<ℓ),\displaystyle=\prod_{\ell=1}^{|y_{t}|}p_{\theta}(y_{t,\ell}\mid P_{\mathrm{slow}}(o_{t}),y_{t,<\ell}),

where Pslow​(ot)P_{\mathrm{slow}}(o_{t}) denotes the slow-path input built from oto_{t}. The LLM first generates the reasoning rtr_{t} and then commits to the action ata_{t} conditioned on that reasoning. The second line expands this process at the token level, where each token yt,ℓy_{t,\ell} is generated auto-regressively conditioned on the preceding tokens yt,<ℓy_{t,<\ell}. Through the transition in Equation 2, the steering action changes the execution state and thereby the actions the executor takes next, steering the system back on track. Execution of the agent system being supervised then resumes until the next observation update.

We write πθslow​(at∣ot)=∑rπθslow​(r,at∣ot)\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{slow}}(a_{t}\mid o_{t})=\sum_{r}\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{slow}}(r,a_{t}\mid o_{t}) for the action distribution of the slow path, marginalizing over the reasoning. Combining the two paths then gives the steering policy in Equation 1:

πθ(at∣ot)=πθfast(It=0∣ot) 1[at=pass]+πθfast(It=1∣ot)πθslow(at∣ot),\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t})=\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fast}}(I_{t}{=}0\mid o_{t})\,\mathbf{1}[a_{t}=\mathrm{pass}]+\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fast}}(I_{t}{=}1\mid o_{t})\,\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{slow}}(a_{t}\mid o_{t}), (6)

where the fast path passes with probability 1−pt1-p_{t} and otherwise delegates to the slow path.

3.3 Reinforcement Learning for Steering Intelligence

Effective steering requires steering intelligence, the ability to assess execution against the overall goal, determine when intervention is needed, and generate actions that bring execution back on track. To unlock this capability for the LLM backbone, we conduct post-training on the steering interface, jointly optimizing the two paths with feedback from task outcomes.

As illustrated in Figure 3(b), the reinforcement learning pipeline samples intermediate states that previous rollouts have reached and lets the steering agent attempt interventions there. The steering agent generates several steering actions at the sampled states, and their final rewards are compared together with those of the unsteered continuations. The comparison teaches the fast path which states carry high steering priority through a pairwise ranking objective, and teaches the slow path which actions improve outcomes through GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). Training keeps the executor frozen and updates only the parameters θ\theta of the steering agent.

Training pipeline.

For each task, an unsteered rollout of the frozen executor initializes a state bank containing the states reached during execution, and the fast path computes a steering priority vθ​(os)v_{\theta}(o_{s}) for every state ss added to the bank with Equation 3, where os=O⁡(g,s)o_{s}=O(g,s) denotes the observation of state ss. The pipeline then performs mm rounds of state selection without replacement. In each round, we select up to kk states, where each selection takes the state with the highest steering priority with probability 1−εsel1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sel}} and a uniformly random state otherwise, balancing exploitation and exploration. At each selected state ss, we sample GG outputs ys,j=(rs,j,as,j)y_{s,j}=(r_{s,j},a_{s,j}) from the slow policy in Equation 5. We apply each steering action to the selected state ss, yielding the steered states {sj′}j=1G\{s^{\prime}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}. To reduce variance, the executor continues the rollout NN times from every state in {s}∪{sj′}j=1G\{s\}\cup\{s^{\prime}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}, and the mean reward over the continuations of each steering action serves as the reward of that action:

R¯s,j=1N​∑n=1NRs,j,n,bs=1N​∑n=1NRs,n0,\bar{R}_{s,j}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}R_{s,j,n},\qquad b_{s}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}R^{0}_{s,n}, (7)

where Rs,j,nR_{s,j,n} is the task reward of the nn-th continuation from the steered state sj′s^{\prime}_{j}, and Rs,n0R^{0}_{s,n} that of the nn-th continuation from the unsteered state ss, averaged into the baseline bsb_{s}. This rollout pipeline provides controlled comparisons among steering actions and the unsteered baseline, allowing the steering agent to learn which states merit intervention and which actions improve outcomes.

Rank-based fast-path learning.

The fast path learns to rank states by steering priority. As the training target, we measure the priority of state ss by the mean absolute outcome change that steering causes relative to the no-intervention baseline,

q⁡(s)=1G​∑j=1G|R¯s,j−bs|.q(s)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\left|\bar{R}_{s,j}-b_{s}\right|. (8)

That is, q⁡(s)q(s) averages how far the GG steered outcomes R¯s,j\bar{R}_{s,j} move from the unsteered baseline bsb_{s}. For the evaluated states 𝒮={si}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{i}\} from the same task, we write zi=zθ​(osi)z_{i}=z_{\theta}(o_{s_{i}}) for the fast-path score of state sis_{i} in Equation 3 and qi=q⁡(si)q_{i}=q(s_{i}) for its measured priority. The set 𝒫={(i,j)∣i<j,qi≠qj}\mathcal{P}=\{(i,j)\mid i<j,\ q_{i}\neq q_{j}\} collects state pairs with different priorities, and di​j=𝟏[qi>qj]d_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[q_{i}>q_{j}] indicates which state ranks higher. We apply the pairwise ranking loss (Burges et al., 2005) for fast-path learning

ℒrank=−1max⁡(|𝒮|−1,1)∑(i,j)∈𝒫[di​jlogσ(zi−zj)+(1−di​j)logσ(zj−zi)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}=-\frac{1}{\max(|\mathcal{S}|-1,1)}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}\left[d_{ij}\log\sigma(z_{i}-z_{j})+(1-d_{ij})\log\sigma(z_{j}-z_{i})\right]. (9)

The loss pushes ziz_{i} above zjz_{j} whenever state ii shows a higher measured priority, aligning the predicted ordering with the measured one, and tied pairs contribute no signal.

GRPO-based slow-path learning.

We optimize the slow path with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) over the multiple steering attempts sampled at the same state. To push steering actions toward positive improvement, we include the unsteered baseline bsb_{s} in the within-group normalization. The advantage of each steering action is calculated by:

Us={R¯s,1,…,R¯s,G,bs},As,jact=R¯s,j−mean⁡(Us)std⁡(Us).U_{s}=\{\bar{R}_{s,1},\ldots,\bar{R}_{s,G},b_{s}\},\qquad A^{\mathrm{act}}_{s,j}=\frac{\bar{R}_{s,j}-\operatorname{mean}(U_{s})}{\operatorname{std}(U_{s})}. (10)

That is, an action receives a positive advantage only when its mean reward exceeds the pooled average of the steered outcomes and the unsteered baseline in UsU_{s}. We assign the advantage to every generated reasoning and action token and apply the standard PPO loss (Schulman et al., 2017):

ℒGRPO=−1|𝒟|∑(o,y,A)∈𝒟1|y|∑ℓ=1|y|min[ρℓ(θ)A,clip(ρℓ(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(o,y,A)\in\mathcal{D}}\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|y|}\min\Big[\rho_{\ell}(\theta)A,\ \operatorname{clip}\big(\rho_{\ell}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\big)A\Big], (11)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} collects the sampled outputs (o,y,A)(o,y,A) across states with their advantages, ρℓ​(θ)=pθ​(yℓ∣Pslow​(o),y<ℓ)/pθold​(yℓ∣Pslow​(o),y<ℓ)\rho_{\ell}(\theta)=p_{\theta}(y_{\ell}\mid P_{\mathrm{slow}}(o),y_{<\ell})/p_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{\ell}\mid P_{\mathrm{slow}}(o),y_{<\ell}) is the token probability ratio against the sampling policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, and ϵ\epsilon is the clipping range.

Combining the objectives of the fast and slow paths, we obtain the training loss

ℒ=ℒGRPO+ℒrank,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}, (12)

which jointly updates the shared parameters θ\theta.

4 Experiments

In this section, we conduct experiments to study three research questions. RQ1: Can a steering agent improve task performance, and can reinforcement learning strengthen its steering intelligence? RQ2: Does the learned steering capability generalize to out-of-domain tasks, transfer to unseen executors, and support controllable intervention frequency? RQ3: Can steering improve a multi-agent system, where goal drift arises from collaboration among specialized roles?

4.1 Experimental Setup

We follow the experimental setting of ASearcher (Gao et al., 2025), which trains on ASearcher-Base-35k and evaluates on seven retrieval-augmented QA benchmarks of multi-hop reasoning and single-hop retrieval with a local Wikipedia retrieval server. We report F1 (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) following the same protocol, with Avg. denoting the mean over the seven benchmarks. For the executor, we use a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct search agent (Qwen et al., 2024), which shows basic search ability but is prone to goal drift. Given the difficulty of the steering task, we use the stronger Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) as the backbone of the steering agent. Further details are described in Appendix A.

4.2 Effectiveness of Steering (RQ1)

To study the effectiveness of the steering agent, we compare it with planning and verification, which use the same supervisor backbone (Qwen3-8B) to decompose the goal before execution and to review the goal completion afterward. Table 1 reports F1 on the seven in-domain benchmarks, together with the corresponding steering cost and execution cost, i.e., steering actions (#Act.) and executor turns (Turns) per task. We adjust the fast path threshold (Equation 4) to keep the average number of steering actions around one per task for a fair comparison.

Zero-shot steering brings the largest gain among the three supervision forms and leaves executor turns nearly unchanged. In comparison, zero-shot planning and verification help less or even degrade performance and lengthen execution. These results show that intervening during execution supervises the executor more effectively than planning ahead or reviewing afterward.

To examine the improvement brought by reinforcement learning, we apply the same learning algorithm (Section 3.3) to the steering, planning, and verification agents. RL improves all three supervision forms over their zero-shot counterparts. Among them, steering benefits the most. RL raises the gain from 1.84 to 6.66 points and reaches the strongest results consistently on all seven benchmarks, with the fewest steering actions and executor turns. These results show that reinforcement learning effectively unlocks the steering intelligence, enabling the steering agent to mitigate goal drift.

Regarding the learning algorithm, we additionally compare online reinforcement learning with an offline alternative, where filtered behavior cloning (BC) (Chen et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2023) imitates the sampled steering actions that improve the task outcome. Filtered BC falls behind our online algorithm, further validating the necessity of online reinforcement learning.

4.3 Generalizability, Transferability, and Controllability (RQ2)

To study whether the learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, we further evaluate on tasks that require an online search API, which exposes more complex real-world information. We test the same steering model without additional training on three more challenging benchmarks that require deeper multi-hop search, namely Frames (Krishna et al., 2025), GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024), and xBench-DeepSearch (Chen et al., 2025a) (Table 2). Steering improves both Avg@4 and Pass@4 on Frames and GAIA, and raises Pass@4 on xBench-DeepSearch. These results show that the learned steering capability generalizes beyond the training distribution. The steering agent mainly learns to recognize and correct goal drift, while task-specific ability stays within the frozen executor, which mitigates overfitting to the training tasks.

To test whether the steering intelligence learned with one execution model can transfer across different model families, we use the same steering model to supervise three unseen executors, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023) and Phi-4 (Abdin et al., 2024). As shown in Table 3, zero-shot steering behaves consistently across the four model families and brings small gains. The steering agent trained with the Qwen executor shows strong transferability, improving the three unseen executors by 15.78, 12.01, and 5.92 points while effectively reducing the executor turns. These results show that the learned steering intelligence transfers to executors unseen during training, allowing the executor to be freely switched without retraining.

We further examine the controllability of the intervention frequency by varying the threshold of Equation 4 at deployment without retraining. We visualize the total gain and the gain per intervention in Figure 4. In the left panel, RL steering consistently improves task performance across all intervention budgets, surpassing zero-shot steering, Filtered BC, and the planning and verification baselines. At the highest intervention frequency, RL steering raises the total gain to 17.11 points. These results show that the fast path design turns intervention frequency into a deployment-time control, allowing the same model to trade steering cost for task performance. In the right panel, RL steering achieves its largest gain per intervention at low intervention frequency, while zero-shot steering and filtered BC remain low across frequencies, lacking the ability to judge where intervention matters most. This demonstrates that the fast path learns to prioritize steering at the states that influence the final outcome most, yielding the largest gain under a fixed intervention budget.

4.4 Steering Multi-Agent Systems (RQ3)

We further conduct experiments on the multi-agent setting. Following TacoMAS (Xu et al., 2026), we build a five-role pipeline for search tasks, where agents with specialized roles collaborate in a fixed order, details of which are provided in Appendix A.4. The observation space of the steering agent is the task goal and inter-agent handoffs. The action space includes appending a guidance note or rejecting the message for retry. The steering agent, the training procedure, and the benchmarks stay the same as in the single-agent experiments. Table 4 reports the F1 metrics, with cost measured by steering actions (#Act.) and agent turns (Turns), the total number of actions executed by agents in the MAS.

Results show that supervising an MAS with lower granularity is more challenging for the steering agent. With the threshold of Equation 4 tuned so that steering actions cover 25% of agent turns, zero-shot steering lowers the average F1 by 1.04 points. Forcing steering at every handoff increases the drop to 7.14 points, with agent turns inflated from 9.2 to 24.1 per task. In comparison, our RL algorithm effectively improves the steering intelligence, achieving gains of 3.90 and 5.34 points under the two frequency settings, respectively. These results show that the same steering interface and learning algorithm are applicable to both fine-grained supervision of a single agent and coarse-grained supervision of a multi-agent system.

5 Conclusion

This paper targets goal drift in LLM-based agent systems and builds a steering agent that decides when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how with a deliberative slow path. Joint reinforcement learning over the two paths unlocks steering intelligence that improves both single-agent and multi-agent systems, generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency. As LLM-based agents and multi-agent systems tackle increasingly complex and long-horizon tasks, the steering agent provides an effective on-the-fly supervision tool to improve their performance and efficiency.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Training Details

Single agent and multi-agent experiments share the same training setup. During training, the steering agent is initialized from Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025). The backbone of the execution agent system is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2024), which is served separately and excluded from parameter updates. We train with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) at a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} and a batch size of 64 tasks for 300 steps. The task reward RR, first defined in Section 3.2, is instantiated as answer token F1 multiplied by a trajectory-format indicator. The F1 term measures the word-level overlap between the predicted and the reference answers, and the indicator is 1 when every executor turn commits exactly one well-formed action tag and 0 otherwise. The remaining reinforcement learning hyperparameters follow the defaults of the ASearcher framework.

Each task performs m=2m=2 selection rounds over the state bank, and each round selects up to k=3k=3 states. Each selection takes a uniformly random state with probability εsel=0.25\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sel}}=0.25 and otherwise the state with the highest steering priority. Every selected state receives its full group of G=4G=4 steering actions. Each steered and unsteered state is evaluated by N=2N=2 executor continuations, whose means give R¯s,j\bar{R}_{s,j} and the baseline bsb_{s} in Equation 7. All new states reached by the continuations are added to the state bank.

We train on ASearcher-Base-35k (Gao et al., 2025), a challenging QA dataset constructed from filtered open-source multi-hop questions and agent-synthesized QA pairs. The training environment is the same local retrieval server as the in-domain evaluation, using the 2018 Wikipedia dump (Karpukhin et al., 2020) as the information source and E5 (Wang et al., 2022) as the retriever.

A.2 Evaluation Details

We follow ASearcher (Gao et al., 2025) to report token F1 on the in-domain benchmarks, and Avg. is the mean over the seven benchmarks. Out-of-domain evaluation runs every question 4 times and reports Avg@4, the mean accuracy over the four runs, and Pass@4, the fraction of questions solved in at least one run. We follow ASearcher to judge answer correctness on these benchmarks with an LLM (Qwen3.8-max (Yang et al., 2025)) as judge, and the judge prompt template is listed in Appendix C.

The in-domain evaluation data of ASearcher (Gao et al., 2025) includes seven retrieval-augmented QA benchmarks, totaling 6,125 questions with 1,000 sampled questions from each benchmark and the full 125 questions of Bamboogle. 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020) builds multi-hop questions from Wikipedia and Wikidata with annotated reasoning paths. HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) contains two-hop questions that bridge or compare Wikipedia entities. Bamboogle (Press et al., 2023) collects hand-written compositional questions that a standard search engine answers incorrectly. MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022) composes questions of two to four hops from single-hop ones with stricter connectivity requirements. Natural Questions (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) contains real search-engine queries answered by Wikipedia. TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) contains trivia questions authored by quiz enthusiasts. PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023) probes long-tail entity knowledge with templated questions built from Wikidata triples.

The out-of-domain evaluation uses three benchmarks that require deeper search over the open web. Frames (Krishna et al., 2025) contains 824 questions that combine multiple constraints and typically require evidence from several Wikipedia articles. GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024) is a general assistant benchmark, from which we evaluate the 103 text-only questions of its validation split. xBench-DeepSearch (Chen et al., 2025a) contains 100 questions targeting the deep-search ability of agents. These evaluations use an online search engine.

A.3 Baseline Design

The planning, verification, and filtered behavior cloning baselines use the same supervisor backbone, and the trained variants reuse the reinforcement learning algorithm, data, and hyperparameters for a fair comparison. The comparison therefore isolates the supervision placement and the learning algorithm.

Planning.

The planning agent is triggered once before the executor’s first action. It reads the same task requirement as the steering agent and writes a plan that the executor keeps in view for the whole task.

Verification.

The verification agent is triggered after the executor commits an answer and decides whether the submission stands. It either passes the answer or rejects it with feedback. The feedback is read by the executor agent as a tool-return, and the executor revises and resubmits. After three rejections the latest answer is delivered without further review.

Filtered behavior cloning.

The filtered BC baseline (Wang et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021) collects the steering actions sampled by the same rollout pipeline as our online RL algorithm and keeps those whose mean reward R¯s,j\bar{R}_{s,j} exceeds the unsteered baseline bsb_{s} in Equation 7. Then it treats these positive samples as the training data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022). The retained pairs of observation and steering action fine-tune the steering agent with a token-level cross-entropy objective (Zelikman et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2023). Compared with our online algorithm, filtered BC is an offline algorithm, so it receives no signal from the discarded negative samples and its training data does not track the improving policy.

A.4 Multi-Agent Instantiation

The multi-agent system adapts the five-role template of TacoMAS (Xu et al., 2026) to search tasks. A planner decomposes the question into subgoals and dispatches them to two searchers, which retrieve evidence in parallel. A verifier reviews the searchers’ deliverables against the question, and a summarizer composes the final answer from the delivered evidence and the verifier’s verdict.

The steering agent reviews a pending handoff using the task, the multi-agent structure, previously delivered handoffs, current handoff, its sender and recipients, and any rejection feedback already issued at that handoff. The action space contains a pass that delivers the handoff unchanged, a note that attaches guidance to the delivered submission for its recipients, and a retry that returns rejection feedback to the sender for revision and resubmission. The full prompt templates are listed in Appendix C.

Appendix B Additional Experimental Results

B.1 Hyperparameters

To study the impact of hyperparameters, we retrain the steering agent varying the number of selection rounds mm, the states selected per round kk, and the continuations per branch NN, keeping the group size G=4G=4 fixed. We evaluate the retrained agents under the in-domain protocol of Table 1 at three target steering frequencies. As shown in Figure 5, all configurations deliver comparable gains at the 15% frequency, staying within a band of one F1 point. When the frequency increases to 50% and 100%, other configurations demonstrate lower performance.

B.2 Cost of the Fast and Slow Paths

To examine the actual cost of the low-cost fast path and the high-cost slow path, we measure their latency on the trained steering agent served by SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). We collect the latency data during the in-domain evaluation of Table 1 and report the average latency per call at 12 concurrent requests per GPU. As shown in Figure 6, the two paths read the same context and therefore share the same prefill cost of about 0.2 s. The fast path then decodes the decision token and finishes within 0.3 s, while the slow path generates about 1.8k reasoning and action tokens on average and takes 30 s. These results show that the fast-slow design effectively separates the cost of judgment from the cost of intervention, allowing the fast path to run at every observation update while the slow path conducts reasoning only when triggered.

B.3 LLM-as-a-Judge Results on In-Domain Benchmarks

To examine whether the in-domain results depend on the token F1 metric, we follow ASearcher (Gao et al., 2025) to supplement LLM-as-a-Judge (LasJ) accuracy for all methods in Table 1. The judge model and prompt template are the same as in the out-of-domain evaluation (Appendix A.2). As shown in Table 5, LasJ accuracy exhibits the same trend as Table 1. The RL improved steering agent achieves the best results consistently on all seven benchmarks, and RL raises the gain of steering from 1.60 to 6.77 points. LasJ accuracy is higher than token F1 overall, as the judge accepts answers that match the reference in meaning but differ in surface form.

Appendix C Prompt Templates

In this section, we list the full prompt templates used in the experiments. Curly-braced slots are filled at run time from the current observation. In the single-agent setting, the slots carry the question, the executor’s rendered action history, the action count with the remaining turn budget, and a line naming the executor’s currently legal actions. A committed note is injected into the executor’s prompt under the header “A steering supervisor has reviewed your progress and left a note for your next action (follow the note):”. In the multi-agent setting, the slots carry the task, the rendered pipeline, the handoffs delivered so far, the submission under review with its sender and recipients, and any rejection feedback already issued at this handoff. The planning and verification prompts share the single-agent context, with the role statement adapted to their placement. The last box lists the LLM-as-Judge prompt of the out-of-domain evaluation.
